Issued at 450 AM CDT Thu Oct 8 2026

Northwest flow aloft will persist over the Northern Plains 
through tonight as a surface high pressure centered over North 
Dakota early this morning slides southeastward. A NW-SE 
baroclinic zone in the wake of the surface high lying under a 
mid to upper level jet places the high temperature forecast at 
around 60 degrees northeast to near 75 in the far southwest. A 
light southerly return flow should keep lows above freezing 
tonight. Strong warm air advection underneath a transient upper 
ridge is expected on Friday, resulting in well above normal high
temperatures forecast to range from around 70 northeast to near
85 far southwest. Lee cyclogenesis downslope of the Northern 
Rockies in response to a potent trough digging into the Pacific 
Northwest will maintain southerly flow with warm air advection 
Friday night, which could keep low temperatures at near-record 
warm values in the upper 40s to upper 50s.

The deepening upstream trough will push the lee surface trough 
into North Dakota as a cold front on Saturday, but the 
strongest low level cold air advection is forecast to lag 
behind. This yields a high temperature forecast from the lower 
60s northwest to the lower 80s in the southern James River 
Valley. Ensemble guidance has come into better agreement on the 
timing of both the surface cold front and the stronger push of 
cold air above the surface. But there are still lower 
membership ensemble clusters that support both an earlier and 
later arrival of the colder air. The leading edge of the colder 
air mass is projected to reach southeast North Dakota Sunday 
afternoon, but there is uncertainty in its magnitude. Two 
clusters composing 60 percent of the total ensemble membership 
favor a warmer solution than the total ensemble mean, while the
other two with 40 percent total membership are cooler than the 
total mean. It is therefore not surprising that the high 
temperature forecast on Sunday has shifted slightly warmer in 
some areas. But it will still be much colder, with highs 
ranging from the 40s far west and far north to near 60 in the 
southern James River Valley.

Dry weather is expected until Saturday night when shortwave 
energy ejecting from the base of a western CONUS trough begins 
streaming over the region. This continues through the day 
Sunday, with low to mid level frontogenesis also supporting 
ascent at times. Through Sunday afternoon, ensemble clusters 
show 2 distinct QPF outcomes that are tied to the temperature 
outcomes mentioned above. The warmer 60 percent solution favors 
lower QPF (around 0.1-0.2") from west central to north central 
North Dakota, while the cooler 40 percent solution favors higher
QPF (closer to 0.25") from southwest to northeast North Dakota.
Precipitation should remain all rain through Sunday afternoon, 
but odds are increasing that will change come Sunday night when 
strong synoptic forcing from DCVA under a split upper jet is 
forecast to arrive. From Sunday evening through Monday 
afternoon, all ensemble clusters show high system-based 
probabilities for exceeding 0.1" QPF and medium chances for 
exceeding 0.25". But there are two distinct spatial footprints, 
with 55 percent total membership broadly painting these 
probabilities across all of North Dakota and 45 percent total 
membership with a narrower axis focused along the ND/SD border. 
When taking into account all ensemble guidance, it is clear that
southwest North Dakota has the highest QPF potential over this 
time period, where calibrated NBM guidance places high chances 
for at least 0.25" and medium chances for at least 0.5". The 
big question then becomes what this precipitation will fall as, 
especially Sunday night into Monday morning when synoptic scale 
forcing is favored to be strongest over western and central 
North Dakota. The bias-corrected NBM deterministic low 
temperature forecast in the upper 20s to lower 30s may be 
slightly too cold, but hourly NBM temperature guidance does 
fall into the lower and mid 30s. This would be supportive of 
snow, perhaps even as a singular precipitation type. But model 
soundings show a deep isothermal layer that could hover around 
the freezing mark. There are other unresolvable potential 
factors at play too, including dynamic cooling of the column 
that could cause a quicker transition to snow and a low chance 
that mesoscale banding could enhance snowfall rates to 
sufficiently overcome warm ground temperatures and allow snow 
to accumulate. Most areas that do receive snow Sunday night 
into Monday morning are likely to see little to no accumulation,
with just a touch of white on the grass. But there is a very
low probability outcome for several inches of snow impacting 
western parts of the state, as evidenced by the shift-of-tails 
in the ECMWF EFI snow output. 

Precipitation should transition back to mostly rain Monday 
afternoon, with chances decreasing from north to south into the
